title: Clinic no-show fee / scheduling policy memo (second-order effects)

items.text: Medicaid managed-care contracts forbid billing members for missed appointments (34% of patients, and the highest no-show group)
paraphrases: Medicaid managed-care contracts say we shall not bill members for missed appointments - the fee can't apply to 34% of patients.
Charging Medicaid members the no-show fee would breach our payer contracts.
The fee is prohibited for Medicaid patients, who have the highest no-show rate (27%).

items.text: Two commercial contracts require 90 days' written notice to the plan before a new patient-facing fee; the memo's 60-day patient notice doesn't cover it
paraphrases: Two commercial contracts need 90 days' written notice to the plan, longer than the 60-day patient notice.
We must notify the commercial plans in writing before introducing the fee.
Commercial contracts impose a 90-day notice requirement that the January 1 date may already miss.

items.text: Text-only reminders won't reach many patients: 15% have no mobile number, 41% have no texting opt-in, and the templates are English-only while 22% prefer Spanish
paraphrases: Automated texts can't go to the 41% without opt-in or the 15% with no mobile number, so reminders actually drop.
Text reminders are English-only but 22% of patients prefer Spanish.
Replacing calls with texts excludes a large share of patients from reminders, which could raise no-shows.

items.text: Equity and access: fees and balance holds deter low-income patients (who no-show most), delaying care and pushing them to the ED or out of the practice
paraphrases: Equity problem: the fee and balance hold fall hardest on low-income and Medicaid patients and deter needed care.
Balance holds create a barrier to access; patients may delay chronic-care visits and end up in the ED.
Penalizing those who can least afford it widens disparities.

items.text: The fee doesn't address the actual causes of no-shows (transportation 38%, work/childcare 19%); fixes for those are missing
paraphrases: The fee doesn't fix the top cause of no-shows - transportation (38%).
Root causes (transport, work and childcare conflicts) aren't addressed; a penalty won't create a ride.
Address why patients miss: rides, flexible hours, easy rescheduling.

items.text: Revenue projections are overstated: Medicaid exempt, first miss waived, 31% collection rate on small charges, and lost patients (9% left after collections) cost more than the fee brings in
paraphrases: The $90k fee revenue is overstated: Medicaid can't be charged and only 31% of small charges get collected.
Patient attrition (9% left after collections letters) loses $148 visits - more than the $75 fee recovers.
Recovering half the $410k by balance holds is unrealistic; expect write-offs and patients leaving the practice.

items.text: Double-booking makes chronic lateness worse: 61% of sessions already run 20+ minutes late, so both-show days cascade delays, wait times and provider burnout
paraphrases: Double-booking the first slot will cascade delays when 61% of sessions already run late.
If both double-booked patients show, everyone waits longer and providers burn out.
Overbooking worsens wait times and can itself drive future no-shows.

items.text: Staff workload shifts rather than disappears: fee disputes, waiver requests, balance conversations at booking, opt-in collection and inbound calls from patients who miss texts
paraphrases: The 30 freed front-desk hours will be eaten by fee disputes, hardship waivers and angry calls.
Staff workload shifts to collecting balances at booking and handling complaints.
Front desk will field inbound calls from patients who never got a text.

items.text: No measurement plan: no pilot, baseline or control, and no tracking of unintended effects (attrition, ED use, complaints, no-shows by payer)
paraphrases: There's no measurement plan: pilot first, set a baseline and track no-shows by payer, attrition and complaints.
No metrics for unintended effects such as patients leaving or ED use.
Evaluate with a pilot and a control group before rolling out practice-wide.

decoys.text: Urgent or same-day sick visits could be blocked by the balance hold
decoys.why_not: The memo states urgent and same-day sick visits are never held for balances.
paraphrases: Patients with urgent needs might be turned away for an unpaid balance.
Balance hold could block same-day sick visits.
Acute care may be denied because of a balance hold.

decoys.text: There is no grace period or hardship waiver
decoys.why_not: First miss each year is waived automatically and leads can waive for documented hardship.
paraphrases: No hardship waiver or grace for a first offense.
The policy should allow exceptions for patients in hardship.
Missing a first-time forgiveness rule.

decoys.text: Patients are not told about the policy in advance
decoys.why_not: Mailed and posted 60 days ahead, and patients sign the updated financial policy.
paraphrases: Patients won't know about the new fee before it starts.
Need a plan to communicate the new policy to patients in advance.
Patients should be notified before the fee applies.
